OUR 

HONORARY 

PRESIDENT 


MISS MARY E. EDGAR 


One of the highlights of the closing banquet of the Canadian and Quebec 
Camping Conference in Montreal, April 9th, at the Sheraton-Mount Royal 
Hotel, was a special announcement by F. M. Van Wagner, the President of the 
Canadian Camping Association. 

The assembled members were delighted to know that Miss Mary Edgar 
was appointed Honorary President of the Canadian Camping Association. As 
director of Camp Glen Bernard for many years she made a very special contri¬ 
bution to the field of Camping and to many Canadian girls and leaders. 

One of her finest contributions to Canadian Campers has been her stories 
and her books of poetry. Our lives have been enriched by her talent in this 
field. 


The Canadian Camping Association has been greatly benefited in many 
ways by her efforts. We are proud that she was the first editor of Canadian 
Camping magazine and, with her Committee, changed it from a mimeographed 
bulletin to a creditable printed magazine. The Magazine has always been one 
of our best efforts in the field of camping. 

It would take many words to relate the many things Mary Edgar has 
contributed to Camping — finances, a field trip across Canada, work on 
several committees. Perhaps one of the ways she has contributed most is in the 
wise counselling she gave to some of those who tried to guide the Association in 
its growth and development. 

As members of the Canadian Camping Association we salute our Honorary 
President, Miss Mary E. Edgar, the members choice. 

Anne 7 . Vail, Past President 
Canadian Camping Association 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1960 


167 


This is an address that was presented at 
the Canadian Camping Association Con¬ 
ference in Montreal, on April 8th, I960, 
at the Mount Royal Hotel, 

RECIPE 

FOR A HAPPY CAMPER 


PROF. ALAN F. KLEIN, 

Professor of Social Group Work, 
University of Pittsburgh. 


I have come to describe to you 
Gamp Utopia — the happy camp for 
the happy child. I am, I think, a 
realist and although everything that I 
suggest cannot possibly apply to every 
camp, much will apply to most. I 
must tell you at the outset that I do 
not believe in too much permissive¬ 
ness, comfort or indulgence, but I do 
believe that research in the behavioral 
sciences has shown us that a regim¬ 
ented, authoritarian and punitive set¬ 
ting is not good either. 

I must begin long before any 
campers, staff, facilities or programmes 
are in existence. The Gamp Manage¬ 
ment must be clear and comfortable 
with its purposes and philosophy. It 
must be explicit as to its values—upon 
these things rests the selection of every¬ 
thing else. I am sure that you will 
tell me that you agree; that this is 
obvious: that you have all this in your 
camp. If you do you are unusual, for 
there is great, great confusion in camp¬ 
ing today, on the operational level re 
the relationship of purpose and how 
the camp is staffed and how it 
operates. 


If you think that camp is a signifi¬ 
cant and valuable experience •— a 
summer vacation plus other important 
factors — it stands to reason that you 
must have the right campers, the 
right staff and the right programme 
for the purpose. 

If you do not screen the youngster 
in intake, group them by plan and pro¬ 
gramme for the purpose, I can only 
conclude that you are fooling yourself 
in thinking that you are clear and 
comfortable about your purpose. If 
you employ callow young staff and 
give them a once over lightly pre¬ 
camp session, I must conclude also 
that you do not mean your purpose. 
For your value should be what you 
care about, really want, set store by 
and will strive for. For example, the 
climate of a camp means more than 
hot sun — cabin groups should be 
developed in which: 

a) a playful, fun-loving, zestful spirit 

is characteristic; 

b) co-operation, friendliness and get¬ 
ting along with others are practised; 


168 


Canadian Gam ping 



c) the basic needs of campers for per¬ 
sonal worth and achievement, be¬ 
longing and status arc recognized 
and met; 

d) wherein responsibility and self- 
governing provide practice and 
growth in self-reliance and respon¬ 
sibility; 

e) reasonableness, open mindedness 
and inter-personal competence char¬ 
acterize the way discussions are 
carried on and decisions made. 

The central factor in such an edu¬ 
cational process — the PLUS most 
camps state that they seek — where 
personal growth, social, moral and re¬ 
ligious development is sought, lies in 
the interaction between persons in the 
situation. 

This leaves it up to you to determine 
who those persons are, who leads 
them, and the situations in which these 
objectives can be reached. 

A. H. Maslow poses for us a hier¬ 
archy of need to be met in any situ¬ 
ation in order to achieve any of your 

PLUS: 

1. Survival — good food — enough 
water, safety and health precau¬ 
tions — freedom from hurt. 

2. Safety needs — these are basic 
security items — freedom from 

fear, anxiety and worry. 

3. Love, Acceptance and Approval — 
this is a critical area. 

4. Esteem needs — favorable reaction 
from others; self-respect — self- 
image — self-adequacy. 

5. Self-realization needs — to become 
one’s best self — to realize one’s 
capabilities. 

One cannot be helped in one until 
there is a minimum satisfaction in the 
others. 


Now we can begin to see that if we 
have certain kinds of facilities and 
staff, the level of needs evidenced in a 
camper may clearly indicate that we 
have no business accepting him, or 
that he needs special attention. 

We can see that intake can also 
help us in grouping, so as to best 
develop our objectives. 

We can see the need for staff selec¬ 
tion and training — and I stress this— 
really thought-out programme. 

Mind you, I have no quarrel with a 
camp wherein the major purpose is 
fun. I do object to slap-happy fun, 
and I do object to fun for staff or 
director with no regard for the 
camper’s level of fun; and I do object 
to fun that teaches evil values and 
that is destructive. 

Whatever your purpose — pure fun 
and/or sunshine and good food — we 
know that it cannot be achieved with¬ 
out understanding. This requires, in 
my opinion, an awareness of the 
developmental levels of children with 
which we work. No one can have 
much fun, or gain any plus value if the 
experiences to which he is being ex¬ 
posed are inappropriate to the age 
level. 

It is well to not hear that liking 
children is not enough. One needs 
both the educated heart and the edu¬ 
cated mind. The counsellor needs to 
be able to think as well as feel; to 
know as well as to like. 

Some years ago Bettleheim wrote— 
Love is Not Enough. Love them and 
limit them. A child who is not limited 
is a deprived child, a frustrated child, 
a rejected child and hence an unhappy 
child. 

turn to page 209 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1960 


169 





THE STAFF MEETING 


ADELE STATTEN EBBS , 
Director: Camp Wapomeo 


It has often been said that a camp is 
only as good as the staff which it em¬ 
ploys. Of course this statement takes 
for granted that all camp directors or 
head counsellors have the same ability 
to train and co-ordinate their staffs. 
And it is true from the campers’ point 
of view that the success of a camping 
season depends on the counsellors. 
These reasons are proof enough that 
there should be opportunities made for 
staff training during the camp period. 
This “in service” training may be a 
review of a previous course, or in some 
cases the only training which is offered. 

The objectives of staff training are 
similar to that of the camp as a whole. 
From the staff emerges the “camp 
spirit”, holiday atmosphere and eager¬ 
ness for activity. The staff can demon¬ 
strate the democratic wav of living in 
a community. The training will demon¬ 
strate the practical application of 
group methods, as well as give insight 
into the needs of individual campers. 
Finally, many programme directives 
will be given, some of which we shall 
develop later. 

There are various ways of training 
staff—all of which should be used. It 
starts with the initial interview during 
the winter, followed up by letters, con¬ 
versations and a few meetings. Pre¬ 
camp is the ideal training ground. At 
that time everyone is focussed on the 
one job at hand—that of becoming an 
effective camp staff member. When the 
campers arrive in camp, there is comp¬ 
aratively little opportunity for train¬ 


ing. However, the success must con¬ 
tinue in various ways. There can be 
personal interviews, plenty of on-the- 
spot supervision (by that I mean ob¬ 
servation followed by conferences), and 
lastly the so-callod Counsellor or Staff 
meeting. 

Meetings called during the busy days 
of camp must have real value. They 
must be informative and to the point. 
Those attending must be the personnel 
really concerned with the subject at 
hand. If at pre-camp all the main 
basic training has been covered, then 
the in-camp meetings will be mostly a 
review. They will give an opportunity 
to demonstrate the general principles 
in practical application. There will be 
general staff meetings of two types: 

(a) A daily review of the day’s pro¬ 
gramme and routine announce¬ 
ments. 

(b) A longer session for instruction of 
a more general nature, followed 
by discussion and evaluation. 

(A) At the Daily Meeting all routine 
matters pertaining to the whole staff 
are highlighted. A brief review of the 
day’s programme is given with oppor¬ 
tunity for synchronizing every depart¬ 
ment. 

Various departments report. The 
Waterfront Director may check on life¬ 
guards for that day, or may announce 
a regatta, asking for the co-operation 
and participation of most of the camp. 
The Dramatic Department may seek 
assistance in some forthcoming project. 
The Dietitian may have something to 


170 


Canadian Camping 






say (or you may have something to 
say to her). On a scorching hot day, 
the nurse can warn against sunburn. A 
recent campwide event can be briefly 
evaluated, or a committee appointed to 
investigate some problem, or to plan a 
function bringing a report back to the 
meeting a day or so later. A standing 
committee of counsellors elected to 
function over a period can handle 
many problems on policy and routine, 
and bring recommendations to this 
meeting. This gives an idea of the 
diversity of the problems that might 
arise. They should be pertinent to the 
whole camp. Matters concerning only 
a few should be dropped and discussed 
later by those concerned. 

“Camp Routines” mimeographed, or 
in a notebook, save a lot of valuable 
time, and can be definite about the 
things over which there can be little 
difference of opinion. These include 
Fire Precautions, Fire Drill, Meal 
Hours, Tuck Shop, Mail, Food Parcels, 
Cash, Days OfF, Sunday Suppers (Pic¬ 
nics), Care of Equipment, Laundry, 
Transportation schedules, Lost and 
Found, Officer of the Day and Night 
Watch schedules. 

A “Staff Organization chart” gives 
guidance to all. The names of the com¬ 
plete staff are included: Counselling, 
Kitchen and Maintenance. If this is 
given out at the beginning of the camp 
it helps to get everyone acquainted, 
and to familiarize the new staff with 
the structure of the organization. 

(B) General Staff Meetings will be held 
less frequently because of the time, in¬ 
volved. It is obvious that during camp 
there is never a meeting at which 
everyone can be present, so the time 
chosen will depend on the individual 
camp. If no pre-camp training has 
been possible, then these topics should 
be introduced as early as possible in the 
season. To decide on the order of their 
presentation is a problem, because all 
arc of vital importance. 


1. Health and Safety —The staff itself 
immediately upon arrival in camp 
must be impressed with the necessity of 
taking every precaution to guard their 
campers’ as well as their own health. 
Simple and clear instructions should be 
given on health routine: daily inspec¬ 
tion, sleep, rest and cleanliness. Pro¬ 
cedures should be discussed to prevent 
sunburn, fatigue, accident from fire, use 
of axes, etc., and routines on the water¬ 
front should be set up. Various staff 
members particularly concerned should 
be prepared to discuss the various as¬ 
pects of camp health and safety—the 
doctor or nurse, the dietitian, the camp 
craft and tripping counsellors, the 
water-front director and so on. A very 
careful briefing must be made regard¬ 
ing the first day of camp. All staff 
members should be alerted to their 
specific responsibilities which start the 
moment the first camper comes under 
camp supervision. 

2. The Role of Camping —This topic 
would give a background to the whole 
business of camping, how and where it 
started; how it has developed through 
the years; where it is heading in the 
future; what it claims to do for the 
campers. This makes the counsellors 
realize that they are a part of a large 
and vital organization on this continent 
today. The Canadian and American 
Camping Associations are becoming 
stronger as people realize what and who 
they represent. These Associations have 
set high standards for themselves, not 
through pressure, but because they are 
composed of a group of people with 
high personal standards. The aims and 
objectives of the individual camp would 
come into this discussion, and to be 
more specific each counsellor should 
have her own objectives and be sensi¬ 
tive to those of her campers and their 
parents. 

3. Programme Planning —Keep in sight 
the campers’ point of view. They are 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1960 


171 




going to camp this summer primarily 
to have fun. It is a holiday—a glorious 
experience away from home and school 
—not only freedom from routine, but 
freedom to explore the realms of 
friendship and human relations. 

Let us analyze a 24-hour day at 
camp. Nine or ten hours of sleep; three 
meals a day takes about four hours; a 
rest period lasts one hour at least; an¬ 
other three hours for routine, such as 
getting up, flag raising, clean-up, flag 
lowering and getting to bed. This all 
adds up to twenty hours, leaving four 
hours for all other camp activities. 
And during this four hours is the only 
chance to find some leisure—some time 
to just sit in the sun and loaf. It is very 
important that during this time our 
campers should have a positive feeling 
of being able to plan it for themselves. 
All the rest of the year these children’s 
standards are set by adults. Some 
homes are quite democratic, but it is 
very hard to find any set of parents 
who can keep themselves in the back¬ 
ground. At school the children have 
practically no say in what they are 
going to learn—or even how they may 
go about it. Camp is the only com¬ 
munity which is run entirely for child- 
dren with the sole purpose of fulfilling 
their needs. Let’s keep it that way. 

Primarily the camp-site itself largely 
determines what activities are going to 
exist and what are going to predomi¬ 
nate. There is usually water enough 
for swimming—but the type and extent 
of the water-craft will differ. So here 
are two factors that have much to do 
with programme planning *— (1) the 
campsite and equipment and (2) the 
aims and objectives of specific camps. 

The two other directives in programme 
planning are more under our control— 
the counsellors and the campers them¬ 
selves. The director need not feel that 
she will be handling the program for 
the campers all by herself; the resources 
of the entire staff should be pooled. 


Campers enjoy having the opportunity 
of getting to know other members of 
the stall—a change is as good as a rest. 
As for the campers’ part in programme¬ 
planning, this is the whole secret of a 
happy and satisfying summer for them. 
We do a lot of talking about the demo¬ 
cratic way of life—of being good citi¬ 
zens in a democracy, and so on. One 
cannot live that life or be a good citi¬ 
zen unless one practices it from an early 
age. At camp we can give the campers 
this opportunity. In order to develop in 
responsibility, independence and ability 
to make wise decisions, we must provide 
varied opportunities for choice. 

In early days of camp, the counsel¬ 
lor’s job was relatively simple. The 
range of activities and resources were 
limited. If there was a champion diver 
or swimmer on the staff — fine; the 
campers surely would learn to swim 
and dive—or else. An Indian in charge 
of canoeing would teach the paddling. 
That is all right up to a point—if you 
can have a champion who also has the 
personality to teach voung children and 
who understands their individual dif¬ 
ferences, their abilities, their fears, their 
emotional development. But to find 
one with the patience, understanding 
and the insight of a trained psychologist 
is difficult. Most activities at one time 
were motivated by the children them¬ 
selves seeking awards. Individual com¬ 
petition dominated the day. Today 
many people do not believe that is the 
best way to get campers to participate 
in activities. But sometimes there is 
such a strong feeling of expectancy that 
everyone will participate in all activi¬ 
ties, that it virtually amounts to com¬ 
pulsory participation. With all these 
external means of motivation there 
would be little opportunity for the 
children themselves to exercise the 
power of making their own decisions. 
So the potentialities for developing into 
strong, thoughful and positive indivi¬ 
duals would be lost. 


172 


Canadian Camping 



4. The Cabin Group — Since this 
group exerts the greatest influence on 
the individual camper, it is important 
that the counsellor be skillful in the 
art of group leadership. The campers 
should be allowed to choose their cabin 
mates whenever possible. The first few 
days are very important. It may be 
necessary for the counsellor to guide 
the group skillfully, suggesting projects 
and enterprises which will knit the 
group together. Each individual must 
develop a feeling of belonging which 
can be increased by responsibility be¬ 
ing given in tasks and decision making. 
There should be a feeling of “give and 
take”. The group experiences should 
be so varied that the same camper is 
not always the leader. Look for oppor¬ 
tunities to bring forward the one who 
shuns the limelight. For the staff meet¬ 
ing one counsellor might be prepared 
to lead a discussion using a specific 
example to illustrate the development 
of this process of “give and take”. 
Experienced leaders could reconstruct 
the situation into a socio-drama. 

5. Spiritual Values —The following is 
developed from the notes of a presen¬ 
tation at a pre-camp course in July, 
1950. There are various approaches to 
the appreciation of nature—that of an 
artist, a naturalist or a geologist. A 
counsellor must make sure that the 
campers, especially the sensitive camp¬ 
ers, have opportunity for quiet commu¬ 
nion. At dawn and dusk this feeling 
or need should have the chance of ex¬ 
pression. In evening discussions around 
the campfire or at bedtime, there 
should be opportunity for quiet talk. 
Tolerance can be developed. There 
should be a feeling of freedom of ex¬ 
pression and sympathetic understand¬ 
ing. At morning meditations another 
opportunity is given for quiet thought. 
Sometimes it may be directed or stim¬ 
ulated by a leader, other times guided 
only by the strains of quiet music. 
There are camp institutions such as 


Council Ring and Chapel services 
which create a receptive atmosphere. 
The democratic way of life has been 
mentioned before. Where can it be 
better understood and expressed than 
at camp. 

The topics discussed above are sug¬ 
gestions to be included in counsellor 
meetings during camp (or in pre¬ 
camp). These may be given to the 
whole staff, or to unit meetings accord¬ 
ing to the age groups with whom the 
staff is concerned. 

Counsellor Meetings can be fun. It 
is a time when the adult group in 
camp can get together and talk in their 
own language. It is extremely valuable 
for building up morale, and reassuring 
every member of the staff that she has 
an important role to play. In finishing, 
may I quote from a letter written by 
Taylor Statten to his staff: “The satis¬ 
faction that a conscientious counsellor 
gets out of working with children is 
very great, and as a result of the 
experience and training one should 
gain some understanding of child 
psychology and group methods which 
we hope will contribute toward a more 
skillful and intelligent parenthood.” 
Books for Reference:

Bill Hamilton a Canadian trapper 
of long ago wrote a book, “My 60 
Years in the Plains” describing the 
dangers of an outdoor adventurous 
life. In it he says, “Give me the man 
who has been raised among the great 
things of nature. He cultivates truth, 
independance, self reliance, and he has 
generous impulses and he is true to 
his friends and to his country . . .” 

This is the type of citizen which we 
hope to be encouraging after a spell 
in our camps! Our camps arc set up 
with elaborate fastidiousness for the 
healthful welfare of our campers and 
we must keep them safe and free from 
harm while they are in our care. Bill 
Hamilton would certainly cock an eye¬ 
brow at our modern methods of adven- 


when it stirs the imagination and there 
is real satisfaction Ln meeting a chall¬ 
enge, overcoming obstacles, following 
a trail or successfully reading a code. 
Naturally the strength of the appeal 
depends entirely on the presentation 
of the game and, of course, a really 
good story adds to the excitement and 
the fun, which to the young, must 
mount to realism. 

The game should rouse the powers 
of THINKING, OBSERVATION, 
DEDUCTION, STALKING, 
TRACKING, SELF-CONTROL and 
ENDURANCE. These arc vital to 
any outdoor adventure and should be 
introduced gradually and by easy 
stages. A simple treasure hunt, look¬ 
ing for coloured objects of different 


ADVENTUROUS CAMES 


turous living, and yet, even to-day it 
is the adventure of living in the great 
o’ doors which has the most appeal, 
from the youngest to the oldest 
camper! Can you visualise that area 
around your camp, and in the shelter 
of the bush or a rock, a young camper 
lying there—scarcely daring to breathe 
and caring not two hoots about the 
uncomfortable position or the mos¬ 
quitos so long as he remains undetected 
by enemy agents, who seem close 
enough to hear his heart beat. The 
secret document hidden in his clothing 
must remain safe in his keeping!!!! 
Such is the thrill of an adventure 
game. The camper, male or female, 
is playing a part and roused by the 
excitement is determined that only 
one side shall win — his. 

There is real enjoyment in an out¬ 
door energetic activity, particularly 


values or noting anything unusual over 
a given route, call it operation ‘Sher¬

vation. Introduce stalking and track¬ 
ing gradually, and the operation has 
become so exciting and absorbing that 
before too long mapping and compass 
are incorporated, night games intro¬ 
duced and even overnight games con¬ 
sidered ! 

BEGIN WITH EASY TRAILS. 
Hunting for treasure is always popu¬ 
lar, and this tvpe of game has many 
advantages. It can be adopted for 
both young and old, can be used for 
any number of players, can be played 
in almost any place and under any 
circumstances, and the time limit can 
be easily controlled. Some ingenuity 
and considerable preparation is neces¬ 
sary in making and laying the clues.

Canadian Camping 




As the campers grow in experience, 
clues should become more difficult. 

THE RAID is another type of ad¬ 
venture game, usually played by two 
teams competing against each other. 
One team may defend a base contain¬ 
ing trophies, the other team attack 
with the purpose of carrying off the 
trophies to some agreed place. A third 
and even a fourth team may be intro¬ 
duced to try to join up with or inter¬ 
cept one or both teams and then an¬ 
other base should be considered. 

GORDON BREAKING is another 
type of game based on the efforts of 
one team to get through a strip of 
country guarded by another team. The 
team trying to get through with the 


(1) There must be a TITLE. It 
does not matter how ingenious the 
game might be, without an imagin¬ 
ative title much of the spirit can be 
lost. The Air Raid, Treasure Cove or 
Operation ‘Sabotage’! 

(2) The THEME or STORY 
should be simple and in no way com¬ 
plicated. Highwaymen, convicts and 
spies are not in the least out of date. 
Inter-Planetary travel can be dreamed 
up by the space-minded. 

(3) METHOD should be kept 
simple. The story should have fired 
the imagination, and players want to 
see it in relation to the game and to 
their surroundings. The teams need 
to plan their campaigns, stalking,

Edith Milne , 

Ontario Girl Guides 


secret document hidden on one of its 
members, guards the bearer of it while 
the other team enjoys intercepting and 
searching the prisoners. 

A MAN HUNT for an escaped pri¬ 
soner, convict or enemy spy can be a 
thrilling game and can be adapted to 
any number, time or place. There are 
opportunities for tracking, stalking, 
disguise and deduction in this type of 
game. 

These four ideas form the basis for 
all adventure games and can be used 
alone or amalgamated depending on 
the experience of the players. It is 
wise to try out the simple ones first, 
making them exciting, with the players 
looking forward to the next time. 

The requirements of an ADVEN¬ 
TURE GAME are:— 


tracking, intercepting, attack defence 
and codes. Identification numbers or 
arm bands for ‘lives* and there should 
be some system for scoring. 

(4) RULES of the game should be 
kept as simple as possible, a detailed 
instruction only makes for confusion. 
The players of each team should be 
counted before and after the game, 
most important! Some method should 
be worked out to reintroduce players 
‘killed* or disqualified, there is nothing 
more miserable than to sit out the 
afternoon while your team is on a cross 
country chase. Reintroduction would, 
of course, be at the cost of some points 
and the points system must be clearly 
understood and it must also be known 
whether a state of ‘mobbing’ will be 
allowed, that is more than one person 
attacking an individual at the same 
time. 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1960 


175 






(5) T I M E and BOUNDARY 
LIMITS will depend on the size of 
the area and the type of game chosen. 
If the game does not cover a wide 
area, a clear cut signal could be given 
to start and to end the game. Bound 
ary limits are very important; roads, 
tracks, woods, fences and any well 
known landmark should be clearly 
defined and in such a way that the 
teams must meet at some stage of the 
game or much of the fun will be lost. 

(6) THE GAME MUST BE 
SUITED TO THE AREA and the 
more adventurous the group becomes 
they may study a map of the surround¬ 
ing area and venture further afield. In 
this case it would be an advantage to 
visit the area with members of the 
group and make a note of landmarks 
and possibilities. A very experienced 
group might even consider using 
canoes and there is no reason why a 
good game should not last overnight. 

(7) HELP is very necessary how¬ 
ever simple the game might be. Clues 
have to be set out beforehand, judge¬ 
ments made during the game and 
‘lives’ may have to be given out — so 
willing helpers are a great asset. 

The success of any adventurous 
game depends entirely on the plan¬ 
ning. The game should include the 
fastest and the slowest members of the 
group. The teams should be given 
time to work out a plan of campaign. 
It is essential that teams really meet 
if they arc supposed to meet in oppo¬ 
sition. A good method of ‘lives’ is 
perhaps for players to wear wool bands 
above the elbows, preferably not 
nylon wool; a different colour for each 
team. At the conclusion of the game, 
the referee or umpire should check 
the points and name the winner. 


Stories which fire the imagination 
make excellent material for adven¬ 
turous games. Scouting for Boys, Out¬ 
door Games for Scouts, tales of explor¬ 
ation and pioneering stories are old 
favourites. 

Adventure Games foster team spirit, 
self control, fair play and obedience 
to rules as well as initiative and self 
confidence; and a good deal of patience 
is required for quiet stalking and lying 
in wait. This indeed is CHARACTER 
training in the wide open spaces of 
camp, FUN and ADVENTURE. 

Smugglers Treasure. Counters to 
represent treasure or diamonds etc. 
Smugglers and Peddlars start, say, half 
a mile apart. Within their own bases 
they are safe. Coastguards start about 
mid-way. Peddlars may only receive 
one counter at any time, and must 
take counter to umpire at a receiving 
base, which, within a- given area is a 
safe place. If Peddlar caught by Coast¬ 
guard, must give treasure and re-enter 
game but if a coastguard is caught he 
must surrender treasure to his captor 
and then count up to, say, 60 before 
re-entering the game. 

S. Boats. This is particularly suited 
to a woodland area through which a 
padh runs and would be an excellent 
night game. At the mouth of the 
harbour, a cord could run from tree 
to tree (the boom.) Two lanterns 
could hang from the trees and on the 
cord two or three flash lights could be 
suspended. Coastal motor boats cruise 
about the channel (path). Steam pin¬ 
naces sail to starting point and make 
for the shore negotiating rocks and 
sea-weed (dead leaves). Coastal boats 
attack in the channel and the S-pin- 
naces try to get through and mine 
the harbour by switching on the 
flashes.

NEWS 


From The Provinces 


FROM ALBERTA 

Not one, but two, conferences did 
those wide-awake camping folk in 
Alberta present for 1960. The first 
for directors in the beautiful setting 
of the Banff School of Fine Arts; the 
second, for counsellors, at Red Deer, 
Alberta, this one sponsored jointly by 
the Alberta Camping Association and 
the Community Recreation Bureau of 
the Alberta Government. Topics gave 
a broad view of camping in that pro¬ 
vince, when Bill Bently dealt with 
Leadership Training, Neil Gamble and 
Jim Hawkes dwelt on Programme 
Development in a practical way, and 
Mrs. S. R. Hughes, Administration 
Officer, Rocky Mountain Forest Re¬ 
serve of the Alberta Government, 
advised directors about Conservation 
and Government Regulations for 
Camps. There were book displays, 
there were movies, there were social 
gatherings, waterfront sessions, Day 
Camp sessions, and Administration and 
Financial Management discussions, as 
well as a valuable talk by Gilbert 
Beatson, Architect, who spoke on Camp 
Site Planning. Out of this came the 
hope that their 1961 Conference can 
be planned early in the year to allow 
administrators of Alberta Camps more 
time to prepare for the operation and 
planning of their sites and pro¬ 
grammes. 


MEETING OF THE CLANS 

Is there a new awareness of camping 
for children in Canada ? Is the increase 
in the number of camps greater than 
we realize? Or is it simply that camp¬ 
ing people in larger numbers are try¬ 
ing to give deeper study to their call¬ 
ing? Whatever the reason, registra¬ 
tions at camping conferences can only 
be called “Legion” compared to other 
years; so, too, with the number of con¬ 
ferences themselves. 1960 saw assem¬ 
blies at Winnipeg, Vancouver, The 
Banff School of Fine Arts, Red Deer 
(Alberta), Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa 
and Halifax, with registration of over 
three hundred and fifty in Montreal, 
and over six hundred and seventy in 
Toronto, with a higher percentage 
than ever before of counsellor dele¬ 
gates. 

A new feeling of unity in Canadian 
Camping pervades the thinking of this 
year's delegates. For the first time in 
the history of Canadian Camping, a 
large number met at the Banff School 
of Fine Arts with every kind of camp 
in Alberta represented. For the first 
time in history, the French-speaking 
groups met jointly, with one of its 
sessions translated from English to 
French. For the first time in history, 
a camping conference programme was 
printed in the two languages.

TIPS 


Kirk A. W. Wipper , 
Director. Camp Kandalore. 


THE 

DIRECT METHOD 


OF ARTIFICIAL RESPIRATION 



It is no longer necessary to outline 
and describe the manifold advantages 
ol the Direct Method of Artificial 
Respiration. This has been accomp¬ 
lished by a number of prominent 
scientists and research organizations. 
Out ol this useful background of know¬ 
ledge must emerge a concern for tech¬ 
niques by which the Direct Method 
can be properly and efficiently pro¬ 
pagated. It is, therefore, the purpose 
of this article to provide some “tips” 
that may serve to assist those who will 
undertake to teach the Direct Method. 
This is also known as Rescue Breath¬ 
ing: Mouth-to-Mouth: or Expired Air 
Method. 

In the first place, it is important to 
be brief and to the point in presenting 
the method to a class. Description 
and discussion should be offered 
following the actual performance or 
demonstration, so that the matter of 
apprehension and misunderstanding is 
removed. The essentials of the method 
may be learned from the following 
simple steps which should accompany 
either “doing” or “watching the 
method being done”. 

(A) To clear the mouth and throat, 
(if necessary), use lingers and/or suit¬ 


able cloth. To drain fluids, turn the 
patient’s body and head to the side. 

(B) To keep a clear air passage, 
tilt the head back (as in diagram), 
and pull or push the jaw up and for¬ 
ward. 

(C) To inflate the lungs, blow 
through the mouth (pinch the nose 
shut), or blow through the nose (hold 
the lips closed). In the case of an 
infant, blow through the nose and 
mouth about ten to twenty times per 
minute. (Ten for adult, to twenty for 
an infant.) 

(D) To be sure you arc operating 
effectively, turn your head after each 
“blow” or breath, and watch the 
patient’s chest rise and fall. Depress 
the stomach if air appears to be 
gathering there. A gurgling sound 
made by the patient during expiration 
may be caused by the tongue falling 
against the back of the throat. To 
correct this repeat or check operation 
“B”, above. 

This language is an example of 
simple, forthright description which 
should not in any way confuse a par¬ 
ticipating group or class. Of course, 


180 


Canadian Camping 




an alert instructor must be prepared 
to enter into discussion and questions 
following the practical introduction. 
To expedite and clarify this process it 
is advisable to have on hand suitable 
diagrams, charts, or graphs. These are 
invaluable aids to the learning experi¬ 
ence, particularly with a topic of this 
kind. 

Finally, there are certain other 
guides which should be pointed out in 
reference to actual participation. The 
author has, to date, experienced no 
real difficulty in presentations of this 
method, but, no doubt, some instruc¬ 
tors may be confronted with special 
teaching problems. To assist in reduc¬ 
ing the possibility of these situations 
these suggestions are presented. 

1. Be sure to ask participants who 
have any kind of cold, throat or similar 
infection to withdraw from practical 
participation. This is an essential step 
to take. 

2. Ask participants to use clean 
handkerchiefs (which they were asked 
to bring), towels or other suitable 
material such as clean bandaging 
which the instructor should have on 
hand. These materials do not impede 
the effectiveness of the method, and 
are a* desirable aid which can also be 
applied in an emergencey. This is a 
technique which does reduce appre¬ 
hension and discomfort of some par¬ 
ticipants. 

3. Do not force or create a situ¬ 
ation in which strangers or members 
of opposite sexes find themselves in 
pairs and may not feel comfortable 
about practice or withdrawal from 
practice. Common sense must be app¬ 
lied here. Certainly the most teach¬ 
able groups are families, married 
couples, groups of relatives, groups of 

turn to page 203 


Yachtsman’s Choice 

The true yachtsman regards sail¬ 
ing as an absorbing hobby not only 
on the water, but on land as he 
cares for his craft and keeps her 
Ship Shape. As a keen devotee, he 
wants his children to follow his 
wake, and to learn at camp the 
proper care befitting a good boat. 
The Gull, designed in mahogany 
plywood for safe family use, is par¬ 
ticularly suitable for instruction a- 
sea and in dock, for children and 
beginners generally. An 11' dinghy 
with mainsail and jib, it possesses 
the unique ability to serve equally 
well as rowboat or motorboat, an¬ 
other feature pointing to its adapt¬ 
ability to camp use. 

Unequalled in her performance 
under sail, she is the fastest in the 
11' class, according to the Ports¬ 
mouth Yardstick; as a motorboat 
or rowboat, her stability is un¬ 
questionable. What could be more 
ideal whether one is sailing or merely 
pottering about? 

No need to worry about a capsize, 
either. In the unlikely event that she 
should keel over, her specially con¬ 
structed watertight hatches form 
bouyancy compartments which keep 
The Gull floating high. She is 
easily righted, even by children in 
The Know. 

Try her out. Ask Mr. Henry 
Croce, of Croce and Lofthouse, for 
technical details. He’s a keen sailor 
himself, and could be easily per¬ 
suaded to take you out, so that you 
can know The Gull’s virtues first¬ 
hand. Incidentally, he is offering 
an unbelievably low price to all 
camp directors. CROCE AND 
LOFTHOUSE ARE AT 21 SUS¬ 
SEX AVENUE, SUITE 47, TOR¬ 
ONTO 5. Mr. Croce can be reached 
at WA. 3-2805.

PADDLING AHEAD 


Kirk A. W. W ip per. 

Chairman, O.C.A. Canoeing Standards. 


This is our latest draft of Canoeing Standards. Incorporated into this new 
outline are many improvements, all of which have been offered by thoroughly 
qualified canoeing enthusiasts. It is our hope that this test series will be widely 
used and that canoe instructors and examiners will find the use of them a real 
asset to canoeing programmes. No doubt there will be other changes made, 
and this will depend entirely on the experience of those who use these tests. 
The newly-formed administrate committee will be pleased to receive suggestions 
that will further streamline the programme. This, however, will not be the 
only function of the committee. 7 he problem of recording and distributing 
awards (cards to start with) must also be faced. Methods of dealing with 
instructor- and examiner-training are further considerations. A set of standards 
cannot survive without appropriate management of such administrative details. 
To this end, no less than thirty five people from at least twenty eight different 
camps will be asked to serve on the new Canoeing Committee organization. We 
tiust this will mean ultimate assistance to all of you who undertake the typically 
Canadian activity of canoeing. 


BEGINNER'S AWARD 


Prerequisite:— Beginner’s Red Cross Swimming Award, or equivalent, with 
ICO yards minimum distance. 


Be Able To: 


Know: 


1. Select a suitable individual paddle (and care for it). 

2. Get in to and out of a canoe correctly. 

3. Kneel in the centre and sit back on heels on floor of the 
canoe. 

4. Sit as a passenger. 

5. Paddle the straight or bow stroke. 

6. Paddle the backwater stroke. 

7. Care for a paddle and a canoe. 

1. Bow, stern, thwarts, ribs, keel, gunwale, painter and decks 
of a canoe. 

2. Grip, blade, shaft and tip of a paddle. 

3. Correct procedure for leaving and approaching a dock or 
beach. 

4. Importance of balance.

Privileges: 


Prerequisites:*

5. Five canoe safety rules. (P. 16, The Canoe and You). 

6. How to trim a canoe for paddling. 

7. Canoe discipline (i.e.—sternsman is In command, bowman 
sets pace.) 

Be allowed to paddle with an experienced canoeist in a canoe 
within a restricted area. 


JUNIOR AWARD 

A knowledge of the Beginners’ Requirements, plus Junior Red 
Cross Swimming Award or equivalent. 

1. Launch a canoe and remove it from the water with assis¬ 
tance at a dock or shoreline. 

2. Demonstrate balance in a canoe. 

3. Paddle bow not less than 200 yards satisfactorily in 
roughened water. 

4. With a bowman, paddle stern for a distance of 200 yards. 

5. Paddle alone satisfactorily in smooth water for a distance 
of 200 yards. 

6. Land a canoe properly at a dock or beach (above). 

7. Experience overturning a canoe, with or without assistance, 
and propel an overturned canoe 50 feet towards shore, 
with or without assistance, using kick or short arm tow. 

8. Paddle an accumulative distance of 3 miles (doubles). 

9. Change paddling side, with permission of sternsman. 

10. Do these strokes: Straight (Bow), “J”, Draw, Sweep. 

1. Correct position and duties of bowman, centre and stern 
paddlers. 

2. Purposes of the strokes named above. 

Be allowed to take out a canoe alone under supervision in a 
restricted area. 

Be allowed to paint brie chevron on paddle. 

Be allowed to go on an organized canoe trip in bowman or 
centre position at the discretion of the Camp Director as 
well as the Head of Canoeing. 


INTERMEDIATE AWARDS 

Junior canoe award; swimming test for Intermediate Red Cross 
or equivalent; paddle (cumulative) distance of 10-15 miles. 

1. (a) Climb in to a canoe alone from deep water; 

(b) Climb in to a canoe from deep water, once with 
partner in water and again with partner in canoe. 

2. Paddle canoe awash, two to a canoe, by hand or with 
paddles.

bow and cross bow rudders, sculling. 

6. Paddle stem satisfactorily J /2 mile in moderate wind. 

7. Paddle alone on one side over a triangular course mile 
long. 

8. With assistance, load a canoe for an organized canoe trip. 

1. Proper care in using a canoe on trips — Portaging, Beach¬ 
ing, Landing, etc. 

2. Proper length and uses of painter. 

3. How to make a minor emergency repair. 

Be allowed to take out a canoe alone, with permission, within 
a prescribed area, under supervision. 

Be allowed to go on an organized canoe trip, bow, centre or 
stern, at the discretion of the Camp Director as well as the 
Head of Canoeing. 


SENIOR AWARD 

Must have had thirteenth birthday, Intermediate Canoeing 
Award, and Intermediate Red Cross Award or equivalent. 
Must have paddled an accumulated distance of twenty 
miles. Must have been on a canoe trip of a least one night’s 
duration. 

1. Swamp a canoe in deep water one hundred yards off 
shore, and with assistance of one other person bring it to 
shore. 

2. Launch a canoe and remove it from the water alone. 

3. Tow an exhausted person with a canoe, in normal paddling 
position. 

4. Do a canoe-over-canoc rescue, with a partner. 

5. Paddle J /2 mile in bow and mile in stern each on both 

sides. 

6. Paddle singly over a set course of one mile, on one side. 

7. Pass a rigid style check on all phases of canoeing up to 
and including the Senior standard. 

8. Demonstrate satisfactory participation in canoe racing. 

9. Climb into an upright canoe from the water, alone. 

10. Lash paddles, and portage a 16' (approx. 70 lbs.) canoe 
correctly, a minium distance of 50 yards for girls, and 100 
yards for boys, (with or without assistance for girls only). 

1. What to do if caught in stormy weather. 

2. How to shake out a canoe full of water with assistance 
(two people take turns). 

3. Load limits (capacity) of canoe being used, (see P. 8 — 
The Canoe and You). 

4. How to cope with bizarre conditions such as squalls, etc. 


184 


Canadi\n Camping 



Privileges: 


Prerequisites: 


Be able to: 


Be able to take out another paddler or passenger within safety 
rules of the camp. 

Be allowed to stern a canoe on a trip under supervision. 

Be allowed to paint a third chevron on paddle. 

MASTER’S AWARD 

Must have passed fifteenth birthday; test must not be com¬ 
pleted before sixteenth birthday (ie. — the equivalent of 
two seasons), senior canoeing award, and senior Red Cross, 
and bronze medallion or equivalent. 

1. Propel a submerged or swamped canoe to shore from 50 
yds. out alone. 

2. Shake out a canoe alone in water over candidate’s depth 
with enough water out to permit successful re-entry of 
canoeists, (fifteen minutes allowed.) 

3. Execute a canoe-over-canoe rescue alone. 

4. (a) Handle a canoe alone in roughened water over a 

triangular course of at least one-quarter mile, keeping 
the paddle on one side in so far as practical. 

(b) Paddle in roughened water to a marker 50 yds. from 
starting point, touch it while going around it; return. 

5. Do two figures of eight, paddling first on one side, then 
on the other. 

6. Paddle Indian style, with paddle in the water, a distance 
of one-quarter mile. 

7. Paddle five miles solo continuously in calm weather. 

8. Show excellent paddling style and care of canoe equipment 
in all conditions. Report to be made of canoeist’s cap¬ 
ability and care of canoe equipment. 

9. Instruct at least three persons in new work in canoeman- 
ship, so that they are able to pass the test for their class. 
(NOTE: Be prepared to demonstrate any of the recog¬ 
nized strokes listed previously, with superior style. 

10. Assume responsibility under supervision for at least a 
two-meal overnight out-trip from the planning to the 
evaluation stages. 

11. Prepare a canoe properly for portaging. Portage it one- 
quarter mile, (except girls; may be two if needed; ^mile for 
boys. Use 16' canoe of approx. 70 lbs. weight). 

12. Choose one of: 

(a) Construction of a practical facility for a typical canoe 
programme. 

(b) Write a short accurate essay on a subject pertinent to 
canoemanship; e.g. — recovering a canoe, critique of 
this, testing programme, etc. 

(c) an efficient and important canoe repair. 

(d) a written examination set by the Canoeing Standards 
Committee of the Ontario Camping Association or by 
the camp administrator.

Toronto, Canada , June , 1960 


185 



WISE 

CANOE 

TRIPPING 


A talk given at the 
O.C.A. Conference, Toronto, 
1960 by Garth A. Kaye, 
Director, Camp Voyageur 


Why does a summer camp conduct 
canoe trips for its campers? This 
important question must be answered 
by the camp administration, and the 
answer must be stated positively and 
definitely before staff can be hired and 
before equipment can be purchased. 
It seems that there are camps that do 
not have a firm policy about tripping. 
Tripping is ofTcred because it provides 
a break from the normal camp routine; 
because other camps have trips and we 
must compete; because someone on the 
staff thinks it would be a good idea 
to take out a trip. Reasons like these 
are not sufficient basis for a canoe 
tripping programme. Campers are 
denied the real benefits and enjoy¬ 
ment that can be had from a good 
tripping programme. 

The canoe provides access to areas 
that cannot be reached by other 
means and thus provides the oppor¬ 
tunity to see and learn about animals, 
birds, plants, weather, stars—in short, 
nature — in a way not possible in 
camp. The need for the skills of living 
together.—r co-opcration, respect for 
others, self-reliance — is dramatically 
brought home to the camper on a 


canoe trip where a small group has 
to exist with no assistance from out¬ 
side the group. Canoe tripping should 
be a means to an end rather than an 
end in itself. 

When the tripping policy of a camp 
is to take advantage < f these oppor¬ 
tunities, many of the present practices 
will disappear. Too often the aim of 
a group on a trip is to go farther than 
the last group, or to cover the same 
distance in a shorter time. The result: 
making camp after dark; poorly pre¬ 
pared and inadequate meals; tired and 
irritable trippers; misuse of equipment; 
inadequate safety procedures and acci¬ 
dents. 

The staff members must be made 
aware of the camp’s policies when 
they are hired! If the applicant dis¬ 
agrees with the director on policy, he 
should not accept the job. As soon as 
he has been appointed trip counsellor, 
it becomes his duty to carry out, to 
the best of his ability, the policy of 
the camp regardless of his own ideas. 
It must be realized by all concerned 
that the trip counsellor on a trip is 
programme director, waterfront direc- 


186 


Canadian Camping 



tor, canoeing counsellor, doctor, chief 
cook, mother, father and friend, all 
rolled into one person. This is a very 
responsible job and requires a person 
who, first, is an exceptional leader, 
and, second, has a high degree of com¬ 
petence in the physical skills of canoe 
tripping and water safety. 

PLANNING THE TRIP 

Who will be going? Camp policy 
dictates that it shall be those eligible 
for the tripping programme. Within 
the group of eligible campers there is 
a wide variation of ability and experi¬ 
ence. The trip has to be planned with 
these factors in mind. 

The length of the trip in terms of 
time and distance will be determined 
by the available routes, the age, 
experience and physical condition of 
the campers. The route should be too 
short rather than too long for the 
time alio ted. Particularly on longer 
trips, one day in four should be allowed 
for lay-over. A lay-over may be neces¬ 
sary because of weather conditions, 
but otherwise provides a day for fish¬ 
ing, relaxing, enjoying the freedom of 
the out-of-doors. 

Safety and emergency procedures 
must be spelled out in detail by the 
camp director before the trip leaves 
the camp. If strict swimming regula¬ 
tions are necessary in camp, then they 
are all the more necessary on a trip 
where we don’t have well planned 
swimming areas and adequate life 
saving equipment. On the water, 
canoes must stay together so that 
assistance can be given in case of 
emergency. A canoe trip leader must 
constantly consider his position should 
a serious accident happen: could it 
have been prevented? Accidents 
usually happen on those trips con¬ 
ducted by two kinds of leaders — those 
at the bottom of the leadership ladder, 


who just don’t know enough to be 
careful, and those far enough up the 
ladder that they consider themselves 
experts and don’t need to exercise the 
required care. A canoe trip is not for 
the leader. Constant vigilance is neces¬ 
sary to prevent accidents, and must be 
exercised in such a way that the 
campers are not denied the fun of the 
trip. Nevertheless accidents can hap¬ 
pen. In case of a serious accident, two 
able staff people are required *— one 
to go as fast as possible for help, and 
the other to stay and supervise the 
rest of the group and to look after the 
injured camper. 

Trips should be planned and equip¬ 
ped so that the campers come back to 
camp in better shape than when they 
left. There is no place for the “What’s 
the matter, can’t you take it?” atti¬ 
tude on the part of trip staff. Campers 
should be sorry that the trio is over 
rather than being glad that they are 
back in camp. If this is to be the 
case, the equipment taken has three 
requirements: to provide a comfortable 
camp, ease in portaging, and facility 
in packing and loading. The first re¬ 
quirement suggests a maximum, and 
the other two, a minimum of equip¬ 
ment. The problem is to find the 
happy medium. 

Good sleeping conditions are of 
prime importance for the health of 
our trippers — there is no infirmary 
on a canoe trip. Flics, mosquitoes and 
rain present a constant problem during 
the summer months. The only satis¬ 
factory protection against these is a 
good tent. A tent, to be of use, must 
be light in weight and large enough 
to be comfortable on a stormy day. 
Sail silk tents, though expensive, 
answer both of these requirements. 
Another “tourist” item, well worth its 
three or four pounds, is an air mat¬ 
tress. 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1960

LIMITED 


For ease in loading and carrying, 
all equipment should be packed in 
similar sized pack sacks. There should 
be no loose article, cameras, shoes, 
paper bags, etc., to be put in the canoe 
at the last minute. These are frequently 
the things that are lost. In packing, 
care should be taken to ensure that 
such things as the first aid kit and 
rain gear can be easily obtained, if 
necessary. 

WHAT ARE WE GOING TO DO 

ON THE TRIP? 

This question does not even arise 
in the minds of many trip leaders, yet 
it is of prime importance to the con¬ 
duct of a good trip. If we are going 
to make use of the opportunities pre¬ 
sented, the question must be given 
careful consideration. 

Frequently, nature lore is difficult 
to teach in camp because there is little 
or no motivation, and it smacks too 
much of school. In the bush, on a 
canoe trip, a knowledge of nature be¬ 
comes useful and important. It ceases 
to be nature study, and becomes 
“knowing the bush”. Why not lean 
against a balsam? What woods are 
good for kindling? What woods are 
good for cooking fire? Which ones 
will burn well when they are green? 
These are important questions on a 
trip. An elementary knowledge of 
meteorology can save a wet night. To 
be able to identify some of the birds 
we see and hear takes on a new in¬ 
terest. It is important to know what 
berries are edible, and to know that 
jewel weed is useful for treating poison 
ivy. Most people are interested in being 
able to name some of the stars and 
to pick out the major constellations. 

Trips should be planned so that 
time can be taken for informal sessions 
about nature whenever the opportunity 
arises. It is surprising how much can

JOIN IN THE SONG 


There is an old legend which tells 
of a palace which mysteriously emerges 
from the earth when a group of people 
all join in the same tune together. 
The singing of your girls at camp may 
not erect a palace where there might 
be a new dining hall, but it can form 
the back bone of a good camp pro¬ 
gramme. 

Music can be fun. Watch the 
sparkle in the eyes of a group singing 
if you’re in doubt about this. 

Music can help create fellowship. 
One of the fastest ways to weld that 
collection of individual girls from dif¬ 
ferent churches in different locations 
into a group is to have them sing to¬ 
gether. 

Music can change the mood of a 
group from hilarity to quiet worship- 
fulness, or the reverse. It is an expres¬ 
sion of a feeling, and group feelings 
can be varied easily. 

Music can teach. Watch for songs, 
the words and interpretations of which 
will contribute to a developing under¬ 
standing of other cultures of people, 
or to a growing idea of God. 


Iris Milton , 

Committee Member , C.GJ.T . 


These things can happen when you 
plan carefully for the music in your 
camp. WHO DOES IT? 

First, there’s the counsellor respon¬ 
sible for leading the music. It isn’t 
necessary to have a great musician, 
but you do need someone who likes 
helping others enjoy music. A sensi¬ 
tivity to the group, and a familiarity 
with songs which will fit and songs 
which will move the group can be 
invaluable. But don’t despair if you 
don’t see that person in the counsellor 
line-up. Leaders can be made. 

The leader gives direction and so 
needs to be in control of the situation, 
ready to start the group together, 
ready to point out the tune and help 
keep the rhythm. A new or inexperi¬ 
enced song leader will want to start 
with familiar songs before attempting 
new ones. Practising in front of a 
mirror will give confidence. 

A NEW SONG 

1. A new friend usually is intro¬ 
duced with some interesting comment 
about the person. Do the same for a 
new song. Briefly tell about its origin 
or about the story it tells. 


Toronto, Canada , June, I960 


191 



2. Whenever possible, a new song 
should be sung to the campers. If this 
seems difficult for some reason, have 
it played on an instrument. 

3. The “trial run” by the girls may 
be just a hum till they become 
acquainted with the words and tune. 
Teach so that the words will be re¬ 
membered and sung wholeheartedly 
without dependence on a book. Songs 
might as well be taught correctly too, 
so watch for little errors and correct 
them immediately. 

THE SONG’S THE THING 

Of course, the selection of songs 
counts for a great deal. Some songs 
serve the'r purpose as safety valves 
and let off steam. Other songs strike 
deep chords of thought and emotion. 
Plans may include a variety such as 
this: 

fun songs—Capital ship (4) 

action songs—Donkey Riding (31) 

folk songs—Wcggis Song (61) 

rounds—Kookaburra (41) 

part songs—the Instruments (19) 

spirituals—Steal Away (77) 

hymns—All Creatures of Our God and 

King (103) 

These arc all found in “Lift Your Voices”— 
see bibliography. 

These are only examples of the wide 
variety available. Something is miss¬ 
ing if new music isn’t added to your 
camp programme and the lives of 
your campers. 

SING—THE WHOLE DAY LONG 
There arc few occasions in camp 
when a song is inappropriate. You 
can sing your way along from the 
first gathering together in the morning, 
through grace at breakfast, songs after 
the noon meal, at interest groups, when 
you go hiking, at vespers and camp¬ 
fire, to a good-night song. 

Some energetic leaders will even 
awaken the campers with a song like 
“Morning Comes Early”. 

Others will use a morning hymn of 
praise like “When morning gilds the 


skies” when the group comes for morn¬ 
ing watch. 

GRACE AT MEALS 

What better way to express thanks 
for our daily food than through song? 
There arc many simple graces which 
are suitable. Watch for them and use 
them. 

BIBLE STUDY 

Music will fit into the study of the 
Bible too. “Go Down Moses” may 
stimulate the thinking for a study of 
that great law giver who had to be 
pushed into doing his job. “Hushed 
was the evening hymn” may serve as 
a reminder that Samuel had an open 
ear, a lowly heart and a deep faith in 
order to hear the voice of God. Our 
selection of psalms will enrich a study 
of the book of Psalms in the Bible. 
One may feel that study of Jesus is 
not complete unless a familiar hymn 
is learned, like “O Son of Man, our 
Hero strong and tender”. 

SONGS AT MEALS 

Many song leaders plan for a sing¬ 
song after the noon meal. For any 
song period it is advisable to have a 
selection made in advance. Start with 
a well known one where all sing to¬ 
gether, before using rounds and divid¬ 
ing your group. A new song is good 
about half way through, when the 
group is “limbered up” and enthusi¬ 
astic. Don’t labour over a new one too 
long. 

While the leader has a list of songs 
ready there are usually some requests 
from the group. There will be times 
also when the mood of the group may 
make it advisable to adapt plans and 
slip in one or two action songs to 
give vent to high spirits. Or, if the 
weather is hot and muggy, you may 
sing less boisterous ones and have a 
few minutes extra rest hour.

from page 192 
INTEREST GROUPS 

There will be some girls who will 
have a special interest in music. They 
may wish to prepare special songs for 
a camp fire programme, put on an 
opera, or learn to lead a sing-song. 
There are folk dances or singing games 
which go along with some of the tunes. 
They are fun to do, and add variety 
Listening to a good recording of a 
great piece of music, after a brief intro¬ 
duction can be a thrilling experience. 

MUSIC IN WORSHIP 

Camp may be a good opportunity to 
help girls find their way around the 
hymnary. One verse of a hymn is 
sometimes suitable for a call to wor¬ 
ship. There arc divisions according to 
theme. Some hymns arc really prayers. 
Some are great peaks of consecration 
or dedication. Help the girls to see 
the different classifications of hymns. 
Use the best in the worship services 
at camp. 

The hymns of our hymn books come 
from different nations through a 
period of many centuries. You may 
wish to use hymns from different 
periods of time or from different 
corners of our world in a special musi¬ 
cal service of worship. 

Incidentally, if there is a new hymn 
needed for the service of worship try 
teaching it during the sing-song period. 

Remember, both words and music 
are important. When we sing at wor¬ 
ship we offer our thoughts to God. 
and any offering to God should be the 
best of which we are capable. 


INCIDENTAL MUSIC 

Hiking will be a part of the camp 
programme to be prepared with a 
couple of good hiking songs like c The 
Road to the Isles”, “Swinging Along”, 
and “Follow the Trail”. 

Antiphonal singing can be a special 
feature too. One group may be on 
one hill and the other across on a hill 
opposite, or one group on the water 
with the other on land. There’s some¬ 
thing very lovely about the voices 
drifting over the air from one group 
to the other. 

CAMPFIRE 

Campfire is traditionally a time for 
singing. Even though the group is 
somewhate scattered, in a variety of 
positions, and the voices tend to drift 
in the open air, there is magic in music 
around a fire. “Rise Up O Flame” 
seems to be an essential part of the 
first cracklings of the struggling flame. 
Songs of evening are plentiful and 
varied. Try some of these •— the hymn 
“The Golden Day is Dying”, the Bo¬ 
hemian “Good Night, Beloved”, the 
Russian lullaby, the round “Whippoor¬ 
will”, the parts joining melodiously in 
“Golden Slumbers”. 

Sometimes you’ll help the group 
visualize the setting of the song. For 
example, mention the negro slaves 
stealing away in the dark after the 
masters have gone to bed, before sing¬ 
ing ‘Steal Away”. 

Yes, there’s no doubt about it. Music 
is a big part of camp—when you plan 
for it.

tian Education, Canadian Council of 
Churches. 

—Camp Interest Group Suggestions—Music 
—Department of Christian Education, C.G.- 
I.T. Committee, Canadian Council of 
Churches. 

—Hymnary.

TASTY SUPPERS 
FOR HUNGRY CAMPERS 

By Elizabeth Steen , B.Sc.H.E.j R.P,Dt. 


Now that summer is rapidly approaching, many plans for your camp 
arc under way. This year, as every year, the problem of feeding your campers 
successfully will be on your mind. After a busy day out-of-doors, a tasty hot 
supper will have sure-fire appeal, especially when the evenings are cooler. 

The following recipes have been used in my operation many times, and 
have proven to be both popular and economical. 

Canned goods have been used in several of the recipes because they 
are easily stored and help speed up preparation time. In each case, large 
oven pans are suggested. The large pans save oven space as well as work in 
serving and dishwashing. However, in most cases individual casseroles may 
be used if desired. 

It is wise to remember that when an oven casserole dish is on the menu, 
a dessert not requiring oven space should be used at the same meal to avoid 
overloading the ovens. 

In the happy camp days ahead, I hope that these supper suggestions 
will prove to be helpful, and a source of enjoyment in your operation.

from page IS8 

he seen and learned incidentally by be¬ 
ing quiet on a portage. Even by tak¬ 
ing a few minutes once or twice a day 
to write up a log of the trip, many 
questions will be asked. Watching for 
and pointing out things in nature is 
very contagious. Because of the in¬ 
formality of this type of teaching, staff 
must be very alert to take advantage 
of situations as they arise. Many good 
field guides to plants, birds, trees, rocks 
etc. are available, can be easily carried 
and arc invaluable on a trip. It is a 
very exceptional person who is an 
expert on all phases of nature. 

Camp should be made in good time 
every day — certainly no later than 
five o’clock — so there is time for a 
good swim and adequate preparations 
for the night. Campfires should be 
planned in the minds of the staff. 
Campers welcome the occasional seri¬ 
ous discussion and it is surprising how 


much sound counselling can be done 
around a campfire. Again much of the 
success of a canoe trip campfire de¬ 
pends on its informality and the leader¬ 
ship given by a good counsellor. A 
good trip programme will not just 
happen; its success or failure depends 
on the calibre of the leaders on the 
trip. A canoe trip leader should be 
working, not holidaying, during the 
trip. 

In closing, a comment about canoe 
trip etiquette. 

How olten do we find campsites 
that are littered with bottles, cans and 
garbage? How pleasant it is to come 
on to a site where the previous party 
had the courtesy to clean up and 
leave a small pile of firewood and a 
well-made fireplace. A motto that 
could well be adopted by every Canoe- 
tripping camp in the country is “We 
leave every campsite in better shape 
than we found it”.

While spices and seasonings are included, these recipes have been used 
successfully in a situation where highly seasoned food would not be accept¬ 
able. It is felt that they would be suitable at camp, but should, perhaps, be 
blander for younger campers. A camp cook will season them to the taste of 
the campers, as his or her experience dictates, especially when the ingredient 
is pimento, onion, garlic, sharp cheese, or mustard.

4. Certain training devices are now 
available, and advice on the avail¬

ever, have not been necessary for 
successful instruction and should only 
be contemplated for use in difficult 
situations. 

5. It is not essential to practice the 
method in order to learn it. However 
some experience is most useful in assist¬ 
ing a sincere participant to appreciate 
the ease and effectiveness of the 
method. It is also instrumental in re¬ 
ducing any apprehension or skepticism 
that may exist. For these reasons, 
practice is strongly recommended. 

In conclusion it should be realized 
that this brief treatment of instruc¬ 
tion problems is by no means either 
complete or final, unusual situations 
may well arise, and these will have to 
be met as they emerge. Advice may be 
sought from organizations who have 
undertaken to teach the direct method. 
Such organizations will also offer from 
time to time other useful ideas for suc¬ 
cessful teaching. In any cases judg¬ 
ment should be based on good common 
sense, so that this old and efficient 
direct technique can be learned and 
used by as many as possible as soon 
as possible.

propagation of the Direct Method of 
Artificial Respiration should be sub¬ 
mitted in writing to the Ontario 
Branch, R.L.S.S., to the attention of 
the author of this article.

HOW DOES YOUR WATERFRONT RATE? 

Kirk A. W, Wipper, Director , Camp Kandalore. 


The check list below cannot be considered an exhaustive one, but it is 
one which I believe to be pertinent to the interests of the well established camp 
that has a waterfront programme. Of course, some items will not apply to one 
or the other type of camp, but in any case, wherever neople are associated with 
activities relevant to waterfronts, the vast majority of pointed questions below 
should be significant. 

There will perhaps be a few who will treat this “check list” lightly and 
say to themselves, “But we have never had a serious water accident at our 
camp!” Statistics, however, tell us quite a different story! Almost every year 
some camp somewhere has a serious accident which may be recorded as a 
“first”. Although, in most cases, blame may not be attached to the camp 
administration, yet somehow there must be a way for us to improve our camp 
to a point, even beyond the remotest accident possibility level. Let us see then 
“How does your Waterfront Rate?” 

PLANNING THE NEW WATERFRONT 

Yes No Are you certain that you have clean fresh water? 

Is the bottom of the area firm, sandy and gradual in slope? 

Have you a stretch of sandy beach or grassy verge leading up to 
the water? 

Are there dangerous cliffs close to your waterfront? 

Is the water usually calm? 

Have you checked with local residents about ice conditions and 
what it might do to a permanent docking system? 

Have you enquired about water level changes during the summer? 
Is the prospective waterfront area free from excessive wind, dangerous 
currents, undertow or tides? 

Have you checked to make sure that at no time are domestic 
animals permitted to wade in or near your prospective water¬ 
front area? 

THE ESTABLISHED WATERFRONT AREA 

Yes No Have you arranged to have your waterfront carefully checked for 
newly acquired hazards, such as roots, stumps, deadheads, etc.? 
Have you arranged to clear away any new accumulation of weeds? 
Have you made plans to remove a movable rock that has previously 
not had attention due to lack of time? 

Have you checked the planking on your docks? 

Have you inspected movable parts, such as hinges, diving board 
fixtures, etc.? 

Are your floating drums free from leaks and your supporting dock 
logs sound and buoyant? 


204 


Canadian Camping 



Yes No Have you set up a defence against swimmers moving under the 
docks and becoming lost or entangled in “under dock construc¬ 
tion”? 

Have you thoroughly examined and measured your one approved 
diving area to make certain that under your 1 metre board 
there is a minimum of nine feet of water, and under your 3 
metre board there is at least twelve feet? 

Have you similarly checked your beginner area for a depth ol 
3 to 3/ 2 feet, your intermediate area for a depth of 3^2 to 
7 feet, and your senior area over 7 feet? 

PERSONNEL AND PROGRAMME 

Yes No Has your waterfront director professional rating? Has your watei- 
front director Red Cross and Royal Life Saving Society or 
Y.M.G.A. qualifications? 

Is he absolutely conscientious and responsible? 

bias he personality as a teacher? 

Has he a thorough and practical knowledge of camping as well as 
waterfront activity? 

Has he confidence and does he display some sense of loyalty to you 
and the camp? 

Have you tried to select other staff members who are qualified to 
serve on the waterfront as responsible assistants? 

Have you provided the waterfront director with a reasonably 
accurate summary of the age and number of campers? 

Have you given him a summary of the equipment on hand or what 
equipment has been purchased? 

Have you outlined clearly to the waterfront director what you 
expect of him; i.e., checking patrols, equipment, progress of 
swimmers, awards, etc., judgment in case of bad weather, etc.? 

Have you established with your waterfront director and all other 
staff members a set of rules and regulations whicn can be 
consistently adhered to through all phases of the camp session? 

Is your checking system thoroughly satisfactory, or should you 
ask for help in its revision? 

Are you providing your waterfront director with time and oppor¬ 
tunity to train the staff (particulaly waterfront assistants), 
in methods of instruction, technique of teaching, water safety, 
artificial respiration, etc.? 

Are you making plans well ahead of time for major events, such 
as regattas, aquacades, etc.? 

For these events have you selected items which are not unduly 
hazardous to participants? 

Have you selected events within the capacity of participants? 

Can all items within your special events be readily supervised? 

Can you be consistent in your waterfront rules and regulations in 
your plan for special events? 

Have you arranged for a pre-camp training session in which you 
and your waterfront director can discuss plans for the summer’s 
waterfront activity with other members of the staff? 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1960

LIGHT FROM A THOUSAND 
CAMPFIRES 

Edited by Kenneth Webb 

Now here is a book to treasure, 
to gloat over and to make you glad 
you arc a camp director — or coun¬ 
sellor. But beware! it will make you 
humble. You directors who pride 
yourselves on your camp, your staff, 
your facilities, your programme—take 
care! It is a book to make you think, 
to make you beat your breast and 
make you wonder What Am I Doing 
In Camping, For Heaven’s Sake? 

Kenneth Webb is a name to con¬ 
jure with in camping circles in the 
first place. (If you have not read his 
“Summer Magic” you shouldn’t be in 
camping at all). This is a compilation 
of what he considers excellent material 
from Camping magazines of the past, 
and if you don’t agree with his choice. 
I miss my guess. 

Fighting our way through the welter 
of new material on camping, we come 
up for air and find Kenneth Webb’s 
book. What a blessed relief! Buy this 
book, read it, think about it, talk with 
counsellors about it—and then read it 
again. And thank your lucky stars 
that there are still so many people who 
believe in camping! G. R. Welch & 
Son. Publishers, Toronto, $5.75.

from page 177 

In Montreal, delegates from Quebec, 
The Maritimes, Manitoba, Saskat¬ 
chewan, Ontario and the United 
States pow-wow-ed about your maga¬ 
zine and urged that editorial commit¬ 
tees be appointed in each province to 
take a responsible part in the collect¬ 
ing and writing of articles and sub¬ 
mitting them to the Editor for ap¬ 
proval by the Central Editorial Com¬ 
mittee. 

An extreme interest in Camp Stan¬ 
dards and Accreditation showed itself 
at the Mount Royal Hotel, when a 
group of members from all provinces 
met to plan for the future. It was 
agreed by Q.C.A. members that camp 
visiting should continue in that pro¬ 
vince, to follow the experimental lead 
ol the Ontario group. Those from 
Manitoba indicated that their Stan¬ 
dards Committee had already set up 
standards, and will continue to follow 
in the footsteps of Quebec and On¬ 
tario. Other provinces are also show¬ 
ing interest in this direction, due to the 
general concensus that an extensive 
educational programme by the pro¬ 
vincial associations, rather than pro¬ 
vincial legislation, is much to be pre¬ 
ferred by camping people in Canada. 

No longer is camping an individual, 
or even a provincial, project. It is 
nationwide. It is an essential part of 
our Canadian life, and each one of us 
must be big enough to give our best 
to its progress, and to use every 
good means available to publicize the 
aims ol C.C.A. and the values of camp¬ 
ing to coming generations. The annual 
Camping Convention is now an estab¬ 
lished event in all parts of Canada. 
Another summer of progress lies before 
us, with, we hope, wider representation 
in 1961 from the provinces at the 
C.C.A. conference in Toronto. Thus 
we can consolidate our aims, and work 
towards “better camping for all”.

from page 169 

In recent years we have relearned 
something else. Erickson refers to it 
as the developmental stage of industry 
in latency (school age) which, if not 
achieved results in feelings of inferi¬ 
ority. Moser paraphrasing Hasighurst 
speaks of the positive attitude to work. 
Recent studies indicate that groups 
must have goals — toward which they 
work — groups and individuals with¬ 
out tasks are likely not to develop 
personalities or to grow. 

This has lead some youth workers 
today to suggest that all groups with 
which we work must have some definite 
purpose towards which they work. 

One of the key factors, which I 
think we neglect, is that of programme. 

Many camps engage a dietitian — 
why? Because a trained dietitian 
knows which foods in what combin¬ 
ations produce a balanced diet for bone 
building, muscle building, energy, etc. 
Then they hire a programme director. 
His or her skill in devising a pro¬ 
gramme menu should be as precise 
as the dietitian’s. You would be appal¬ 
led if your dietitian served constant 
large helpings of sweets and starches 
because “that’s what the children 
like” — or served spicy delicatessen 
nightly even though many campers 
awoke with cramps and bad dreams. 

Why is it presumed that any pro¬ 
gramme is good or that a programme 
director needn’t know one from the 
other? You lads and lassies from 
Physical Education — you are fine 
cooks but untrained as dietitians in 
most instances. 

To the extent that one understands 
the characteristics of activity can one 
select programme for the purpose or 
for reaching your objectives.

from page 209 

The task is one of selecting activities 
with maximum impact in the desired 
direction. Even if you can’t do that, 
at least you can avoid programme 
that is harmful. It strikes me that 
often the institutions that are most 
interested in the spirit pay far more 
attention to the bodily needs than to 
the spiritual ones in the way they run 
their camps. 

To have a happy camper there must 
be a happy camp. A happy camp is 
based upon three major factors: 

1. Common agreement with the goals. 

2. Conviction that the leadership will 
help us reach our goals. 

3. Agreement that the methods being 
used will get us to where we want 
to go. 

This is the essence of morale. 

—• 


Please Note! 

Bill 32 of the 1st session of the 26th 
Legislature of Ontario states that 
“Section 61 of the Public Lands Act, 
as amended by Section 2 of the Public 
Lands Amendment Act of 1955 is 
further amended by adding thereto 
the following subsection: 

“Where public lands over which a 
portage has existed or exists have 
been heretofore or are hereafter 
sold or otherwise disposed of under 
this or any other Act, any person 
travelling on waters connected by 
the portage has the right to pass 
over and along the portage with his 
effects without the permission of or 
payment to the owner of the lands, 
and any person who obstructs, 
hinders, delays or interferes with 
the exercise of such right of passage 
is guilty of an offence, and on sum¬ 
mary conviction Is liable to a fine 
of not more than $100.”

Camp as a return to nature for chil¬ 
dren brought up in urban culture 
How to realize a camper's potential 
through your program 
The rewards from working with handi¬ 
capped children

For this and many reasons, you'll wont to own 
LIGHT FROM A THOUSAND CAMPFIRES. In its 
glow, you will find light shed upon a whole new 
world—a world of comradeship, joy, strength, 
romance, laughter, beauty and understanding. 
Camping is the cultivation of the richest potential 
of the human spirit. For anyone whose lively 
curiosity sparks an inteicst in all that concerns 
children, this book will have a deep and lasting 
significance. 



"CAMPING IS 

EDUCATION" 

We have no question but that this 
will prove to be a classic of camping 
literature. Many letters of praise have 
been received, one of which states 
that "the message contained is of such 
an important nature that it should be 
mailed to every person in the country 
connected with education."

THE UNIQUE MISSION 
OF THE SUMMER CAMP 

In the words of Fred Rogers, AC A 
President: "Would that every camp 
related person might read this beauti¬ 
ful treatise on camping. In these 
days of materialism, urbanization, 
mechanization, conformity, and super¬ 
ficial living, it is good to have the 
Dean of Camping, C. Walton Johnson, 
bring into clear focus the real purpose, 
philosophy, and mission of the sum¬ 
mer camp."
